## I1
One-Sentence Story: Identical average success rates can conceal opposite rankings of robot memories when evaluation is conditioned on observationally indistinguishable histories requiring different actions.
Theme: Evaluation and Diagnostics
Form: problem discovery with initial mathematical investigation
Summary: Define a history-alias class as prefixes sharing the current observation but requiring different terminal actions under verified simulator rules. Define alias-balanced error by assigning equal weight to each required-action class within each alias class. The research claim is descriptive: aggregate success does not identify alias-balanced error, and published rankings may reverse under this explicitly defined target distribution. It makes no claim that a particular architecture or memory mechanism causes failures. An analytic two-class construction in E5 proves non-identifiability; the new research payoff is an identified evaluation object and a reproducible test of ranking stability over actual task histories. The system does not propose a repair module.
Minimal Falsification Experiment: Freeze five existing memory policies E1–E5 and four benchmark families. Generate 800 held-out alias sets using only simulator transition rules; audit 100 randomly chosen sets with exact state replay. Evaluate identical actions and trajectories for every method with shared seeds and equal memory/action budgets. Report ordinary success and preregistered alias-balanced error with stratified paired confidence intervals; release all class membership and oracle labels to permit audit. Use the strongest validation-selected policy as the ranking reference. A label-shuffle control must erase class-specific rank reversals; a non-alias matched set controls for difficulty. First paper: two researchers, two GPUs, 24 GPU-hours, no retraining. Kill the empirical instability claim if no pairwise reversal survives simultaneous intervals or if alias labels are unreliable. The expected signal is a ranking reversal, not a gain from a new controller. No intervention-based causal explanation is promised.
Why It May Be Novel: E6 gives a concrete non-identifiability witness. E1–E5 report aggregate or naturally frequency-weighted slice metrics; none identifies the alias-balanced target or tests rank invariance under it. The contribution's value depends on whether the new target corresponds to genuine history-dependent deployment decisions.
